item.title: I stopped fighting anti-cheat on Linux and started using Steam Remote Play, and I don't miss dual-booting
item.itunes:title: I stopped fighting anti-cheat on Linux and started using Steam Remote Play, and I don't miss dual-booting
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Linux runs nearly everything I need now, and for that reason, it's my daily driver OS. There are exceptions, and they're almost exclusively games that require an anti-cheat client that doesn't play well with Linux. These are games like EA Sports FC 27, Escape From Tarkov, Battlefield 6, and most other competitive games. Those games also happen to be some of my most played titles, which is why I've kept around a Windows install on a second drive for the better part of a couple of years.

I've since stopped the constant swapping between operating systems and started streaming those games to a secondary PC. My gaming PC now stays in Windows and streams those games to a mini PC running Ubuntu using Steam Remote Play's Pyrowave codec. It feels close enough to local that dual-booting just doesn't feel worth it anymore.

Moonlight and Apollo help me experience my PC games the console way

My PlayStation is shaking in terror

By  Samarveer Singh

Anti-cheat on Linux is a fight that I can't win

It's a dead-end at the moment

Proton has made actually running most of my library on Linux a non-issue, but it can't fix a game whose anti-cheat refuses to run. Escape From Tarkov uses BattlEye, which can work under Proton only when a developer opts in, and Battlestate Games hasn't. Battlefield 6 and EA FC 27 use EA's Javelin anti-cheat, which runs at the Windows kernel level and requires Secure Boot, and both games are marked as "Unsupported" on the Steam Deck.

So, the choice is clear: skip those games entirely if I leave Windows for good, or just constantly run a dual-boot setup. I chose the second option, but that extra bit of friction has resulted in me consistently forgoing a session and instead starting up a different game that will run cleanly on Linux.

Linux gaming's next leap isn't more FPS, it's a working Wayland overlay

Overlays are responsible for more than just friends lists and screenshots

4
By  Ty Sherback

Why Pyrowave makes streaming more workable than the older Remote Play

Locally, it's always been good enough for casual titles, but competitive games are more playable now

Remote Play has always been capable of streaming games between PCs for years, but it has always felt like you're streaming a game, even in casual titles. I recently played Dinkum through Remote Play on my MacBook Air, where it's not supported natively, and even with a solid Wi-Fi 7 connection near the router, I still experienced some stuttering and visual artifacts during gameplay. It's fine for a game like that, but for anything competitive, it's unacceptable.

Pyrowave is what enables Remote Play to be much more adept at streaming faster-paced games locally. It's an experimental codec that takes the opposite approach to most video codecs like H.264, HEVC and AV1. Those codecs keep bitrates low by predicting each frame from the ones before it and then packing the result down with heavy entropy coding. That's efficient, but the downside is that it takes time to encode and decode, and a lost packet can leave artifacts on screen until a clean frame arrives.

Pyrowave is intra-only, meaning every frame is compressed on its own like a still image. It has very simple entropy coding and runs entirely in Vulkan compute shaders on the GPU, and the result is encode and decode times of well under 1ms at high resolutions like 4K. The cost is bandwidth, and Valve says it can use five to ten times as much of it as other streaming codecs, and recommends wired gigabit Ethernet at a minimum.

I won't use anything but Steam for PC gaming because of this one feature

I primarily play games through Steam for this single reason.

8
By  Rich Edmonds

The codec is what makes it feel local

It's like I'm sitting at my desk

My setup is a bit unconventional, but it's a good candidate for Remote Play. The gaming PC sits in my office, but the Minisforum MS-03 I run Ubuntu on is in another room of the house that I also like to work in. If I want to run a quick game of EA FC 27 or do a quick Tarkov raid, I can just stream it directly from the more powerful Windows PC.

I still feel some latency, but it's surprisingly playable. In Tarkov at 4K and 120 FPS, Steam's overlay reported 8.38ms of display latency with no frame loss. Battlefield 6 came in at 13.64ms at around 97 FPS. EA FC 27 has very similar numbers, and in that game particularly, you can't feel the latency much. To set this up for yourself, the process is quite simple: both machines need the Steam Client beta, the Linux side needs the experimental SteamRT3 client turned on in Steam's settings, and Pyrowave gets enabled in Remote Play's advanced client options before you start streaming.

The obvious objection here is the fact that I could just walk across the house and and play on the Windows machine natively, but if you really didn't want to leave a Linux environment to play your favorite anti-cheat-enabled titles, this is one of the only ways to do it. Additionally, if I wanted to play these games from my couch on my HTPC running CachyOS, I wouldn't be able to without employing Remote Play like this. In the case of something like EA FC 27, this isn't just the perfect setup, but it's the only setup.

Linux gaming is getting faster because Windows APIs are becoming Linux kernel features

As time goes on, fewer games than ever are unplayable on Linux

18
By  Ty Sherback

It's Windows with more steps, but the point was never to fully escape

I still run a Windows machine at my main setup, but with virtually all of my work living on Linux, not having to switch between them in a boot menu feels great. The client PC is a very small, quiet machine that can handle all of my daily duties, and for the games that won't run (and probably wouldn't run well) on it natively, Remote Play with Pyrowave is the new answer.

item.title: I let Codex take over a project Claude Code couldn't finish, and it caught issues Claude missed
item.itunes:title: I let Codex take over a project Claude Code couldn't finish, and it caught issues Claude missed
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Whenever Claude Code finishes a build, it will let you know, and the file usually opens and will mostly work. What it doesn't tell you is what's off with the first look, and if you don't actually write code, like me, then there isn't much to check it against. Reading line by line isn't realistic for me so I have to rely on testing the build and asking the agent what's happening underneath.

OpenAI publishes an official plugin that puts Codex inside Claude Code, which seemed like a cheap and easy way to get a second opinion without leaving the window. A second set of eyes that can actually read the code made more sense than a second set of mine, so I built a test project and gave Codex the file Claude had already called done.

I switched from Claude Code to Codex for a week, and the trade-offs surprised me

One week, two tools, a lot of opinions.

29
By  Mahnoor Faisal

What "done" actually means in Claude Code

The problems that never throw an error

Claude Code is good at getting a file that runs, but where it tends to let me down is what happens after the fact when a job gets reported as done but something still feels off. In a landing page I built with Fable 5, for example, the background animation was supposed to be a scatter of shards. Claude Code confirmed they were spawning and called the page done, but on screen they were huge with borders that made them look like loose buttons, and it took two rounds of asking before they stopped looking like that.

Edits are another thing. I can ask for one small change and Claude tends to adjust things I never mentioned, so fixing one problem tends to leave me with even more, or just a course of direction for the project. These quirks won't throw you an error, Claude will still report success. So the only way to notice the issue is when I look at the right part of the build and catch it myself - or get a second opinion, because I'm almost certainly bound to miss something on my own.

Claude Code works best when you stop asking it to code

Claude Code became far more useful once I stopped treating it like a code generator and started using it to understand projects and terminal chaos.

11
By  Jeff Butts

Handing my projects from Claude to Codex

Pulling a second pair of eyes into the same window

OpenAI built a plugin that lets you hand off work from Claude directly to Codex. It works by calling the Codex command line tool you install on your PC and using that tool's login, so whatever Codex does comes out of my ChatGPT plan and not Claude's. A ChatGPT account is needed (the free one counts) or an API key, plus Node.js 18.18 or newer.

You start by logging into Codex. Then inside Claude Code, type /plugin marketplace add openai/codex-plugin-cc followed by /plugin install codex@openai-codex, and it asks how widely the plugin should apply (I picked the narrowest option, so just the folder I was working in).

Using it comes down to /codex:rescue plus a description of the job. A small Claude helper will pass that to Codex, which works in the background, and the answer shows up in the same window as a message from Codex.

What a second model found in a file Claude had finished

Reviewing a project Claude called done

The project here was called DVD Shelf, which is a one-file tracker for a DVD collection with a dark mode that remembers your choice. I used Opus 5.5 on Medium, and it handed it to me as finished.

Then I passed it to Codex through /codex:rescue with instructions to review everything and change nothing, and the list came back in seconds. Keep in mind, I didn't configure a model, meaning Codex would have defaulted to codex-mini-latest, which is optimized for speed and instruction following.

For one, the page would have completely crashed if the stored collection was anything other than a clean list of DVDs, or even if any entry was missing a title. Then there were the garbled characters - some of the icons in the file were broken replacement characters that would have rendered as unreadable boxes in the browser. Claude wrote them in and moved on, but Codex noticed.

What followed was more about accessibility functions. The decorative initial on each DVD cover was being read aloud by screen readers before every title, since there wasn't anything to tell it to stay quiet. Clicking a genre stat updated the filter but then also broke keyboard focus because the button would get replaced in the re-render. Search result counts would update on-screen, but not in a live region, so screen reader users wouldn't have been able to hear anything change.

I wouldn't have caught all of these things by using the page myself. I think Claude built it more like a human would have, with a mouse on a clean file and none of my own data in it yet.

Claude Code installed my IDE, and now I can't go back to manual setup

I can't believe I was working in hard mode

1
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Not every project needs to stay with the tool that started it

I still default to Claude for building my projects, primarily because it's where my rules and skills already are. But sending my builds to Codex for a read-through seems like the smart thing to do now, because I wouldn't be able to catch all the bugs myself, and Claude will likely make changes I didn't ask for during the iteration process. This whole handoff came to about 5% of my Claude usage that day, which isn't too bad, but it was a pretty small project so the jury is still out on larger ones.

Codex
See at Github

item.title: I replaced my aging Shield TV with Onn's budget box, and it handles Plex better than Nvidia's streamer
item.itunes:title: I replaced my aging Shield TV with Onn's budget box, and it handles Plex better than Nvidia's streamer
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I love my Nvidia Shield TV Pro, but I recently decided it was time to replace my seven-year-old streaming box. The only thing currently on the market that comes close to its performance is the Onn 4K Android TV budget box. It has newer hardware than the Google TV Streamer, which is still too buggy. Not to mention, the price was quietly increased by $50.

Don't get me wrong: the budget Onn box can't replace a self-contained Plex server or its two USB ports, but as a client, it handles Plex better than the Shield TV. Even after tweaking the Shield TV's settings to improve its performance, I find the Onn handles self-hosted media from Plex better.

A better client device

The 2026 Onn 4K Streamer is responsive when playing Plex media

Since I've started using the Onn box, I've found it to be a better everyday streaming device for watching my Plex library. The Shield TV remains a more-than-capable streaming device for a home theater, and it still hosts my self-hosted media library, which my Onn and other devices play. But I have replaced the Shield TV at the TV level. I still have it on in the background full time via developer options.

The $60 Onn 4K Android TV box features 3GB of RAM, 32GB of storage, Wi-Fi 6, and Dolby Vision support. For such a low price, it can handle Plex media as a dedicated device. Especially since I don't have a mixed library of random media files I found online, which Plex then organized for me. My files are properly ripped from DVD and Blu-ray to MKV, and I've had no trouble playing anything.

The Android TV Plex app loads content fast, and I can skip through movies and shows without a hiccup. Some owners have noted trouble with a lack of lossless audio passthrough support, but I've played more than 50 HDR files and haven't noticed any sound issues. I did have some issues with playback while it was connected to Wi-Fi. However, I hardwired it via its Ethernet port and haven't had trouble since.

Onn 4K Pro Streaming Device
$60 $60 Save $0
$60 at Walmart

Onn's budget box and Plex

It's surprisingly good at loading and playing content

For an affordable box, the Onn launches Plex fast; it loads my library and posters fast and provides responsive playback control. I tested it with 1080p and UHD 4K Blu-ray content, as well as my older DVDs. Content starts immediately after you press play; the picture is crisp, the audio sounds great, and buffering is minimal (since switching to Ethernet).

The 2026 Onn box is more responsive than the Google TV Streamer despite being less powerful on paper. The 4K Pro Streamer has a newer chipset, which avoids the bottlenecks included with the nearly three-year-old Streamer. I can play Plex content much faster and more easily with the Onn box. It doesn't have dual USB 3.0 ports, but it does include a single USB-A 2.0 port for plugging in drives for local media playback.

Where the budget box falls short

It doesn't outperform the Shield TV, but it makes an affordable client replacement

The Shield TV still beats the Onn box in several key areas. The Shield TV Pro supports Dolby TrueHD and DTS-HD passthrough, AI upscaling, and, of course, two USB 3.0 ports. The budget box includes only a single USB 2.0 port, which you can expand with a powered USB hub for additional local media viewing. The Onn's Ethernet port is also limited to 100Mbps, whereas the Shield TV has Gigabit Ethernet. This can be a problem for specific demanding local files, but so far I haven't had an issue with it handling Plex content.

It also doesn't include the Shield TV Pro's gaming capabilities. So, if you rely on the Shield TV for its GeForce Now cloud gaming, the Onn box isn't a good choice. It is for handling Plex content, though. The Shield TV acts as a Plex server and client; however, I have retired it as a client. I am only using it as a server now because the budget Onn box handles Plex so well. It hasn't replaced every convenience I enjoyed with the Shield TV Pro, which is why I haven't completely abandoned the Shield TV, but it is the new client in my setup.

This budget Android TV box is making me rethink streaming sticks

With more functionality and a cheap price, I might never consider a streaming stick again.

By  Brian Burgess

Replacing the Shield TV with the Onn 4K Pro Streamer

The Onn budget Android TV box doesn't outmuscle the Shield TV in any way. However, it does make a great replacement for a client in my room where I want a responsive way to browse and watch my Plex library. Sure, the Shield TV is still running as a server, and I still use it.

But for $60, it's hard not to make the case for this affordable device as a Plex client. It doesn't have the top-of-the-line specs; it's a budget box after all. Still, it is more responsive than you'd think and plays my Plex library served from my Shield Pro.

item.title: I replaced Microsoft 365 with free open-source apps, but this one app is hard to leave behind
item.itunes:title: I replaced Microsoft 365 with free open-source apps, but this one app is hard to leave behind
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I’ve used Microsoft 365 for years, so moving away from it felt like a bigger experiment than simply uninstalling a few apps. I wanted to see how far I could go with free, open-source software without making my daily workflow harder. Instead of looking for one package to replace everything, I tested different tools for different jobs and used them long enough to see where they actually fit. Everything worked more smoothly than I expected, but one part of the experience made me realize just how much I had taken a certain Microsoft app for granted.

LibreOffice made me question my choice

It challenged my need for Office

LibreOffice is the first replacement that really makes me question whether I need Microsoft 365 at all. When I started using it, I expected plenty of compromises, but most never became a problem in my daily work.

Writer handles the documents I create regularly, and I don't have to change much about how I work. Calc gives me everything I need for the spreadsheets I actually use, while Impress works well for the occasional presentation. The interface feels familiar enough that I can open any of the apps and get started without spending time learning a new workflow.

I did notice some differences when working with Microsoft Office files, especially with formatting, but they haven't been enough to make me switch back. LibreOffice continues to handle my everyday office work without a subscription, and it has become a perfectly practical replacement.

Nextcloud replaced OneDrive

I took back control of storage

Nextcloud is another replacement that fits into my workflow without requiring much adjustment. I mainly use it to keep my files available across devices, much like I did with OneDrive. Once I had it set up, I could access the same folders from my desktop, browser, and other devices whenever I needed them.

What I like most is that my files are no longer tied to Microsoft's cloud. I decide where the data is stored, how much space I want, and which folders I want to sync. The desktop client also keeps the experience familiar because files appear directly in my file manager instead of forcing me to manage everything through a browser.

It isn't completely maintenance-free, though. Since I'm running Nextcloud myself, updates, storage, backups, and occasional troubleshooting are now my responsibility. Still, that trade-off works for me. Nextcloud gives me the cloud storage experience I need while giving me much more control over where my files actually live.

This one free open-source tool replaced three paid apps I'd used for years

I thought free office suites always came with compromises, but this open-source tool proved I was completely wrong.

1
By  Yash Patel

Joplin feels like the perfect OneNote

Note-taking without all the clutter

Joplin turned out to be one of the easiest Microsoft 365 replacements for me. I mainly wanted a simple place to write, organize, and find my notes, and Joplin covers those needs without making things unnecessarily complicated.

I organize my notes into notebooks, add tags when needed, and can quickly search through everything when I need to find something. The editor also feels comfortable for everyday writing, so I didn't have to completely change how I take notes. I especially like that Joplin uses Markdown, which keeps my notes portable instead of locking them into a proprietary format.

Another thing I appreciate is how flexible the app feels. I can use it across my devices and keep my notes organized in a way that makes sense to me. It doesn't try to turn note-taking into a huge productivity system, which I actually prefer.

After using Joplin for a while, I stopped thinking about what I was missing from OneNote. For my note-taking needs, it simply works.

Half-baked new Outlook made me switch to Thunderbird

Thunderbird became my way out

New Outlook is where my Microsoft 365 replacement experiment takes an unexpected turn. I had already moved away from Microsoft's other apps, but I still wanted a dependable email client. Unfortunately, the new Outlook experience doesn't feel like the Outlook I was used to.

Some of the changes felt unnecessary, and I found myself spending more time adjusting to the new interface instead of simply managing my email. It also feels less like the complete desktop email client I had relied on for years. That was enough to make me look elsewhere.

Thunderbird became the obvious option because I wanted something straightforward and open source. After installing it, I connected my email accounts and got back to basics without dealing with Microsoft's ecosystem. The interface isn't identical to Outlook, but that's not really the point for me. I want an email client that stays out of my way and gives me control over how I manage my inbox. Thunderbird isn't perfect, but it fits my current workflow better.

I replaced my entire Microsoft 365 subscription with free open-source apps

The zero-dollar productivity stack

41
By  Parth Shah

I still miss Classic Outlook

After replacing almost every part of Microsoft 365, Outlook is the one app I still genuinely miss. Classic Outlook wasn't perfect, but it was fast, capable, and felt like a proper desktop application. I only realized how much I valued that after switching away from it.

What frustrates me is that Microsoft already had something that worked. Instead of improving the experience I liked, the new Outlook feels slower, more bloated, and increasingly focused on features I don't really need.

Thunderbird works well enough for me, and I don't regret moving away from Microsoft 365. But I still hope Microsoft remembers what made Classic Outlook so good. I don't need more AI features or another redesign. I just want Outlook to feel fast, stable, and useful again. That's the version I'd happily come back to.

item.title: I dropped 900GB of duplicate files across my home server, and the tool that found them was free
item.itunes:title: I dropped 900GB of duplicate files across my home server, and the tool that found them was free
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have close to 10TB of data on my NAS, including backups and a large movie library for Jellyfin. Some of that storage is used to keep multiple copies of the same files, and I’m responsible for a fair bit of it. item.itunes:title: 6 "old" CPUs worth buying in 2026 because they work with the RAM you already own
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's no secret that the last 12 months have been terrible for buying PC hardware. From RAM and SSDs to graphics cards, everything has reached record prices, thanks to the global silicon shortage. CPUs, however, haven't seen major price hikes, which remains a silver lining for those looking for an upgrade. However, the total platform cost that comes with it has spoiled the party for DDR5 enthusiasts.

Those of you already using a previous-gen, DDR4-based system can instead look toward AM4 and LGA 1700 processors. These CPUs are compatible with the DDR4 RAM you already have in your rig, and they aren't bad buys by any definition. At the right price, whether brand-new or pre-owned, these "old" CPUs can be great drop-in upgrades for both modern gaming and productivity.

We thought Chinese companies could save us from the DRAM crisis, but they're charging just as much as the big three

CXMT is playing by the same rules as Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron

9
By  Ty Sherback

Ryzen 7 5800X3D: The fastest AM4 gaming chip

No holds barred

The recently relaunched Ryzen 7 5800X3D remains both iconic and powerful even in 2026. The first chip to truly show the potential of AMD's 3D V-Cache, the Ryzen 7 5800X3D still trades blows with modern 6-core chips from Team Red. Despite chips like the Ryzen 7 7800X3D and 9800X3D handily beating it in gaming performance, the Ryzen 7 5800X3D is still a decent pick for AM4 users.

If you're switching from any Ryzen 1000, 2000, or 3000 CPU, then the Ryzen 7 5800X3D will deliver a massive boost to your framerates. Most AM4 motherboards can support this chip with a BIOS update, allowing you to upgrade your PC without paying for a new motherboard and RAM kit. The only caveat is the price. The Ryzen 7 5800X3D has shot up on the used market with listings exceeding $400.

Instead, a brand-new 10th-anniversary edition of the Ryzen 7 5800X3D can be bought for around $350 on multiple ecommerce platforms (at the time of writing). It's not a small investment, especially on a dead platform, but it's certainly cheaper than a full platform upgrade, which probably won't outperform the Ryzen 7 5800X3D anyway.

This workstation chip still packs a punch in productivity workloads, and is obviously no slouch in gaming either.

While it launched at $550 in 2020, you can find it on eBay for around $250 today. That's a steal for a CPU of this caliber, and it can last you for a while. The upgraded model, i.e., the 16-core, 32-thread Ryzen 9 5900XT, is regularly available for around $300 if you want something even more powerful.

By  Rich Edmonds

Ryzen 7 5700X: The budget upgrade

Ideal for most gamers

For those of you who want an affordable upgrade over your existing AM4 chip, the Ryzen 7 5700X is undoubtedly one of the best options. I've been using this chip for over four years now, and it hasn't let me down. I've paired it with the RTX 3080, and it has allowed me to enjoy the latest AAA games at smooth framerates at 1440p. This 8-core, 16-thread CPU has a meager 65W TDP despite being a decent productivity chip.

Using PBO, you can extract the most out of it, and I've been able to overclock it for some extra juice, too. Its gaming performance is almost identical to that of the Ryzen 5 5600X, but it's possible to buy it at the same price, too. If the difference is significant, then I'd advise going for the 6-core chip. Used models are currently a no-go for the Ryzen 7 5700X, since they cost as much as buying it new on Amazon.

6-core gaming doesn't have to be lackluster

You don't need the Ryzen 7 5800X3D to enjoy AMD's 3D V-Cache in your games. The significantly cheaper Ryzen 5 5600X3D provides virtually the same performance as the Ryzen 7 5700X3D, and sits just below the Ryzen 7 5800X3D. If you want a gaming-focused chip without spending over $300, the Ryzen 5 5600X3D can be had for just $220 (at the time of writing). It's relatively harder to find, but you can try your luck on Micro Center and Amazon.

The Ryzen X3D magic fails to impress with budget and mid-range GPUs

By  Tanveer Singh

Core i5-12400F: The budget pick for Intel users

If you wish to join Team Blue

Intel's 13th and 14th Gen processors were mired in controversy due to an infamous bug causing high voltages, which dealt lasting damage to the silicon. The older 12th Gen chips, however, were Intel's comeback as Alder Lake showed what a hybrid core architecture could do. The Core i5-12400F was one of the best gaming CPUs when it launched, and 4 years later, it's certainly not old.

The 6-core, 12-thread CPU (no E-cores) is as fast as the Ryzen 5 5600X in gaming, and costs the same on the used market ($125–$150). It's a starter 12th Gen chip, so it only makes sense for those building a budget PC from scratch. This means buying a cheap LGA 1700 DDR4 motherboard and 16GB/32GB of RAM, but at least you won't have to shell out a small fortune for DDR5 memory. And you have the option of swapping your motherboard for a DDR5 model while retaining the CPU.

Whether it's gaming or productivity you want on an Intel system, the Core i7-12700KF won't disappoint. At the time of writing, it's still available brand-new for around $220 on sites like Amazon.

This 8 P-core, 4 E-core chip is powerful enough to last you a few more years while you wait for the market to settle down. When it does, you can consider buying a DDR5 motherboard and RAM kit for a sweet performance boost. LGA 1700 is a dead platform, just like AM4, but that doesn't mean it's useless in 2026.

It's not the right time to shop for new CPUs that require selling your kidney to afford a DDR5 memory kit. Instead, upgrading to a capable AM4 CPU or building around an LGA 1700 chip can save you money without a massive drop in performance. There's no lack of options on either platform, and those with an already compatible PC need only a good deal on an older CPU to avoid the inflated PC hardware market.

item.title: I used only free software for a month and found 5 apps worth keeping
item.itunes:title: I used only free software for a month and found 5 apps worth keeping
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have reached a point where almost every useful app seems to come with a subscription attached. Individually, a few dollars a month doesn’t sound like much, but stack enough of them together, and the bill starts getting ridiculous. So, I decided to run a simple experiment: for an entire month, I would avoid paid software wherever possible and rely only on free alternatives for my everyday work and personal tasks.

Most of the apps I tested didn’t make the cut, but these five were good enough that I am keeping them installed even after the experiment ended.

I replaced Notion, Google Tasks, and Figma with one Obsidian setup, and now I can’t go back

I built my perfect productivity hub

1
By  Parth Shah

Obsidian

My notes finally felt completely mine

Obsidian was one of the easiest apps to keep after this experiment. It does offer paid services, but I don’t really need them for my workflow. My notes are stored locally as Markdown files, so I can put my vault inside the cloud storage service of my choice and keep everything synced across my devices.

I use Google Drive for this, which gives me the convenience I need without adding another subscription.

My biggest hesitation with Obsidian used to be its mobile experience. The desktop app has always been excellent, but the Android and iOS apps never felt quite as polished as the competition. That changed with the recent redesign.

The developers have done an excellent job modernizing the interface with a floating bottom bar, and I now find the mobile experience good enough. The desktop app is still where Obsidian really shines.

Markdown gives me complete control over my notes, while community plugins let me expand it almost endlessly. I can visualize connections with Graph view, brainstorm in Canvas, build databases with Bases, manage tasks, and customize practically every part of the experience.

Obsidian
OS
Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, iPadOS, Android
Individual pricing
Free normally; $4/month for Obsidian Sync

Obsidian is a robust PKM tool.

Download Obsidian

Flow Launcher

Windows navigation suddenly became much faster

The Windows Start Menu always felt basic to me. It works fine for launching an app or digging through a few settings. But when I need something more specific, it feels slow. Flow Launcher fixed it almost immediately.

I now use it as my main way to get around Windows. A quick keyboard shortcut brings up the search bar, and from there I can launch apps, find files, run a quick calculation, and even trigger web searches without touching the Start menu.

It feels much closer to Spotlight on macOS, but with far more room to customize how it works.

Flow Launcher

Flow Launcher is an open-source alternative to Windows Start Menu.

See at Flow Launcher

OnlyOffice

A free suite surprised me

OnlyOffice was one of the biggest surprises from this experiment because I expected to miss Microsoft Office almost immediately. Instead, I got comfortable with it much faster than I thought I would. The interface feels familiar, the layout makes sense if you have spent years using Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, and I never felt like I had to relearn how to do basic things.

The biggest win for me is document compatibility. OnlyOffice handled my existing documents well enough that I could keep working without constantly checking whether something had shifted or broken.

It also covers the everyday tools I actually use, including formatting, comments, track changes, tables, spreadsheets, presentations, and even templates.

Microsoft Office is still more powerful overall, especially once you get into advanced Excel and PowerPoint workflows. But for my day-to-day writing work, OnlyOffice gets the job done.

OnlyOffice

OnlyOffice is an open-source Microsoft Office alternative.

Download OnlyOffice
I don’t pay for productivity apps on Mac, I use these open source tools instead

Boost your Mac productivity without spending a dime

4
By  Parth Shah

PDFGear

PDF editing stopped feeling unnecessarily expensive

PDF software is one of those categories where I always expect the useful features to be locked behind a subscription. PDFGear was a pleasant exception. I started using it for the basic stuff, but it quickly became my default PDF tool because it handles far more than simple viewing.

I can edit text, add or remove pages, merge PDFs, split documents, add signatures, and reorganize pages without constantly running into a paywall. That covers almost everything I need for invoices, contracts, article references, and other documents I deal with regularly.

The interface is also clean enough that I rarely have to hunt around for the tool I need.

PDFgear

PDFGear is a free PDF editing tool.

See at Official Site

Affinity

Creative work without another monthly subscription

Affinity was an easy inclusion on this list because its value proposition has become almost ridiculous. Canva acquired Affinity in 2024, and the company has since taken things much further by making the new Affinity completely free.

I don’t need professional design tools every hour of the day, but I regularly work with images, graphics, thumbnails, and other visual assets. Affinity gives me the precise editing and design controls I don’t get from basic image editors.

I can work with layers, masks, selections, typography, RAW images, and more without feeling like I am using a watered-down alternative. Some premium AI features are still tied to paid Canva plans, but the core experience remains free.

Affinity
OS
Windows, macOS
Developer
Serif (Canva)

Affinity is an all-in-one design tool for professionals.

Cost
Free (optional paid subscription)
See at Affinity

Free tools I would happily recommend

This month reminded me that ‘free’ doesn’t automatically mean ‘worth keeping.’ I tried plenty of well-known options, including Joplin, Bitwarden, LibreOffice, GIMP, and several others, but they didn’t quite fit my workflow well enough to make the final cut.

Some felt dated, some required too many compromises, and others didn’t give me a strong enough reason to switch from what I was already using.

Obsidian, Flow Launcher, OnlyOffice, PDFGear, and Affinity were different. Each one solved a real problem without constantly reminding me that I was using a free alternative. I kept reaching for them even after the novelty of the experiment wore off.

item.title: My Raspberry Pi now fixes itself when services die, and I haven't SSHed in weeks
item.itunes:title: My Raspberry Pi now fixes itself when services die, and I haven't SSHed in weeks
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I recently built a small network setup using a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. It handles all the inbound DNS queries with a combination of Unbound and Pi-Hole. There are additional Docker containers for monitoring and a dashboard. I've also deployed Tailscale outside these Docker containers for remote access and use Tailscale Serve whenever necessary. The overall setup works nicely, and I've rarely noticed a major outage. But when that happens, my first idea is to SSH into the Raspberry Pi to check what's wrong.

Such incidents urged me to think of a script that runs in the background, scanning the system for any inactive services. The purpose of the script would be to keep an eye like a watchdog and self-heal all the tools without my intervention. Let's explore how the script works and why you should use one on your SBC.

DNS availability matters

But tools are unpredictable

When you think of something network-related, like the tools I have on my Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, the biggest concern is uptime. Ideally, the server should never face any downtime, but that's not always the case. A glitched service, process, or Docker instance can render the server unusable. If I'm on my PC or have the dashboard open in a browser window, I can check which containers are currently down.

But that's not a good idea when every search query from my PC goes to the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W server. I'm waiting for an incident to occur and then work on fixing it. Some services like Tailscale don't even show up on the dashboard because they're deployed outside of Docker. If it fails, I can no longer access the system when I'm not at home.

Setting up a local DNS was one of the easiest improvements I made to my home network

Having local control opens up so many possibilities

14
By  Joe Rice-Jones

So, the server needs a mechanism that's able to find such problems and try to fix them. A script is the simplest way to achieve a self-healing server, at least for the most common issues. It’s lean, configurable, and can run at boot, making automations much easier. Systemd is a great way to schedule and launch scripts, and I use it for my Raspberry Pi and Ubuntu server as well.

Creating the script

Factoring in the smallest details

Most users build some kind of tracking and alert system that sends notifications when the Docker or server is down. It tells you about the issue but doesn't do anything to restore it to a working state. The other major problem is the system resources available on the SBC I picked for this project. A Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W can run my whole setup without any problem.

However, it cannot run tools like Uptime Kuma, Grafana, and a few others. A script is wise because it loads at startup and runs in the background at small intervals. I tested with both Gemini and ChatGPT to come up with a script for this goal and used the one from the latter. It uses a lot in between checks and doesn't restart the server at the first error encountered.

I use these 5 tools to turn my Raspberry Pi into a self-hosting behemoth

Even a Raspberry Pi can become a containerization war machine with the right set of apps

By  Ayush Pande

The script first checks whether Docker is active or not and then moves on with container status inspection. It restarts everything that's not running. Then it checks whether Pi-Hole is active with a DNS query before attempting a restart. Unbound gets a similar check, and then the Tailscale service is analyzed.

Even if everything works, the internet could be down, and there's a check for that too. The script initiates a system reboot only when multiple checks fail and saves a log file. There's a timer to force the script to run after a short duration. The main reason for that is not to have it continuously running in memory because it's a luxury for the SBC.

Docker has internal checks

The script goes beyond it

Docker already supports restart policies, and you can check them in the configuration file. But merely restarting the container won't check for other problems that exist on the server. I use the restart policy for all my containers, but the script acts as an additional layer of protection. It manages the complete Docker system along with Tailscale and external network connection checks.

The script checks whether Pi-Hole actually works and tests the Unbound DNS resolver. If anything seems out of place, it gets logged, and then the script tries to fix it. Similarly, if a Tailscale process exists, that doesn't mean the service is actually active. It restarts the service to make it functional again. Docker doesn't implement any checks outside the containers.

I built an always‑on VPN gateway with a Raspberry Pi Zero to access my home lab from anywhere

It's perfect when I want to work on my home lab projects from external networks

item.title: HDMI eARC is the only audio port on your TV that matters, yet most people plug their soundbar into the wrong one
item.itunes:title: HDMI eARC is the only audio port on your TV that matters, yet most people plug their soundbar into the wrong one
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
HDMI has been the predominant way to connect streaming devices and soundbars to TVs for decades. With HDMI ARC's introduction in the late 2000s, the standard further simplified the TV-soundbar connection, eliminating the need for a separate audio cable between the two. A few years later, HDMI eARC ports started appearing on smart TVs, allowing you to enjoy native content from your TV in uncompressed audio on your soundbar.

A potential hiccup is that many people still don't use an HDMI eARC port to connect their TV to the soundbar. They keep using older HDMI ARC ports, either out of habit or because they don't realize the eARC port has greater bandwidth. Modern lossless audio requires the right HDMI port (and cable) to function as intended.

It's easy to assume all HDMI ports on your TV are identical

You pay dearly if you use the wrong port

Unlike what you might think, most users aren't too excited about diving into HDMI specifications before they can start enjoying their new TV and sound system. This naturally opens the door for a "wrong" connection, where the user plugs in their soundbar into the first spare HDMI port they find on the TV. The probability of this port being a standard HDMI ARC port is high, since most TVs still have a single HDMI eARC port.

The difference between an HDMI ARC and eARC (enhanced ARC) port is the maximum bandwidth. The former supports only about 3 Mbps, while the latter can carry up to 37–38Mbps. This extra bandwidth is necessary to send uncompressed audio, such as Dolby Atmos and DTS:X, to your soundbar. This means HDMI eARC ports are the only ones people should consider when streaming modern content on expensive soundbars.

Your TV is hiding its best HDMI port, and it's probably disabled by default

It might be why your PS5 doesn't perform like it should.

4
By  Samarveer Singh

Most soundbars make HDMI eARC a non-negotiable

Most people don't have premium soundbars

The more practical reality of the HDMI ARC vs. eARC situation is that most people can't do without at least one eARC port on their TV. Picture this: if your soundbar has both HDMI in and HDMI out ports, you can plug your streaming device into the HDMI in port and connect the HDMI out to your TV. You're essentially bypassing the TV's HDMI setup, so whether it has an HDMI eARC port becomes immaterial—just your soundbar just needs one.

Most people, however, don't enjoy this luxury. Budget soundbars still feature only HDMI out ports, forcing people to connect their streaming device directly to the TV. This makes an HDMI eARC port on the TV essential if you want to route lossless, uncompressed audio to your soundbar.

If you don't have an external streaming device and use your smart TV's built-in apps instead, HDMI ARC is enough to handle the compressed Dolby Digital Plus audio from streaming apps. However, as soon as you add a 4K Blu-ray player or media server, eARC becomes necessary for a premium audio experience.

The HDMI cable matters just as much as the port

Don't reuse old HDMI cables

Even if your TV has an HDMI eARC port, the wrong cable can cause unexpected issues with lossless audio and video. Regular HDMI 2.0 cables, even those rated for 18 Gbps, may not fully support uncompressed audio, depending on the cable quality and length. You should aim for an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable, which officially supports 48 Gbps of bandwidth, enough for lossless video and audio formats.

Cables rated "HDMI 2.1" don't necessarily mean anything, since you can't tell the supported bandwidth or whether other features are properly implemented. The "Ultra High Speed HDMI" specification guarantees that you're buying a higher-grade cable instead of random inferior ones simply labeled "HDMI 2.1."

These HDMI cable mistakes were costing me picture quality without an error message anywhere

They could be why your display looks worse than it should

By  Samarveer Singh

HDMI eARC should not be treated as a luxury in 2026

Some manufacturers still skip an HDMI eARC port on modern TVs, especially on budget and lower mid-range models. Since most people rely on streaming apps, standard HDMI ARC ports are enough. That said, brands shouldn't get away with skipping a key HDMI feature in 2026. More and more people are building their own media servers at home, and eARC is a must to enjoy lossless audio and video.
